title: Constrained Decoding
scopeHtml: Scope: Forcing valid output formats with grammars and schema-constrained decoding, and its trade-offs.

notes.title: Why free generation cannot promise a format
notes.html:
In plain words. A language model does not "write JSON". It picks one small piece of text (a token, roughly a word fragment) at a time, over and over, until it decides to stop. Nothing in that loop knows about brackets, quotes or your field names. It only knows "given everything so far, which token is probably next". Most of the time the probable token is the correct one, so the output looks perfect. Occasionally it is not.

Why this matters. Your code calls json.loads(reply) or deserialises into a data class. One stray character breaks the whole request. Typical failures seen in production:

  • Chatty wrapper text: Sure! Here is the JSON: before the object.
  • Markdown fences around the answer.
  • A trailing comma, a single-quoted string, an unescaped newline inside a string.
  • A field renamed (user_name instead of username) or missing.
  • A value of the wrong type ("42" instead of 42) or an enum value invented by the model ("URGENT" when only HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW exist).
  • Output cut off in the middle because the token limit was hit.

Constrained decoding (also called structured generation, grammar-constrained decoding, guided decoding, or "structured outputs") fixes the first five at the source. Instead of asking the model nicely and checking afterwards, the serving engine takes away the model's ability to choose a token that would break the format. The output is valid by construction, not by luck.

This note is about the mechanism underneath. See also the existing C3 notes 02_S1 (structured output basics, function calling, validation, schema design); here we go into how the masking works, the grammar machinery, the engines, and the trade-offs.

Without constraints:   prompt --> model --> any token --> maybe-valid text --> parse --> (fail?) retry
With constraints:      prompt --> model --> logits --> MASK invalid tokens --> sample --> always-valid text

Real products and papers. OpenAI "Structured Outputs" (2024), Gemini responseSchema, Anthropic structured outputs (verify the current feature name and availability in the Anthropic docs), llama.cpp GBNF grammars, vLLM guided decoding, the Outlines library and its paper "Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models" (Willard and Louf, 2023), XGrammar (MLC / CMU, 2024), Microsoft Guidance.

Real life. Free generation is a person writing on a blank sheet; constrained decoding is a form where the pen physically refuses to write outside the boxes.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the model is trained to output JSON, so it is always valid". Training makes it likely, not guaranteed.
  • Confusing constrained decoding (engine-side, changes sampling) with prompting for JSON (model-side, only a request).
  • Thinking retries are the same thing. A retry costs a full extra call and can fail again; masking cannot fail on syntax.

notes.title: Decoding basics: logits, softmax and sampling
notes.html:
You need three words before the mask makes sense.

  1. Vocabulary. The fixed list of tokens the model knows. Modern models have roughly 30,000 to 250,000 entries (for example around 128,000 for a Llama 3 class tokenizer; verify for your model). A token can be a whole word ( the), a fragment (ing), a single character, or punctuation, and many are several characters such as {" or ":.
  2. Logits. At each step the model outputs one raw score per vocabulary entry. Higher score means "more likely next". They are not probabilities yet and can be negative.
  3. Softmax and sampling. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities that sum to 1: p_i = exp(z_i) / sum_j exp(z_j). Then the sampler chooses one token: the largest (greedy), or randomly weighted by probability, possibly after temperature scaling (z / T), top-k (keep only the k best) or top-p (keep the smallest set whose probability reaches p).
loop until stop token:
    logits = model(tokens_so_far)        # shape [vocab_size], e.g. 128000 numbers
    probs  = softmax(logits / T)
    next   = sample(probs)
    tokens_so_far.append(next)

The key observation: the sampler is ordinary code between the model and the output. It sits outside the neural network, so the serving engine can change what it sees without retraining anything. Constrained decoding is exactly one extra step inserted into that loop.

Why not just fine-tune the model to always emit JSON? Fine-tuning raises the odds (many providers do this) but cannot make them 100 percent: sampling is random and a 0.1 percent chance per step compounds over hundreds of tokens. A hard guarantee needs a hard mechanism, which is the mask.

Real life. The model is a contestant giving each possible answer a score; the sampler is the judge who picks. Constrained decoding is the stage manager who removes the wrong answer cards before the judge looks.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing temperature 0 guarantees valid JSON. Greedy still picks the most likely token, which can be a chatty one.
  • Forgetting that logits are per token, not per character. Grammar rules are about characters, tokens are chunks of characters (a big source of bugs, covered later).
  • Mixing up logits (raw scores) and probabilities (after softmax).

notes.title: Logit masking step by step
notes.html:
The core trick. Before softmax, compute the set of tokens that are legal at this exact position. Set every other logit to negative infinity. Since exp(-inf) = 0, those tokens get probability exactly 0 and everything legal is renormalised.

Worked numbers. The generated text so far is {"age": and the schema says age is an integer. The model, being chatty, wants to say Sure. Four candidates and their logits:

token   logit   legal here? (integer expected)
Sure    3.0     no
4       2.0     yes
7       1.0     yes
}       0.5     no

Unconstrained softmax:
  exp: 20.09, 7.39, 2.72, 1.65      sum = 31.85
  P(Sure)=0.631  P(4)=0.232  P(7)=0.085  P(})=0.052
  -> 63 percent chance of breaking the format

After masking (illegal logits = -inf):
  exp: 0, 7.39, 2.72, 0            sum = 10.11
  P(4)=0.731   P(7)=0.269
  -> always a digit, and the relative preference 4 vs 7 is preserved

Check: 7.39 / 10.11 = 0.731 and 2.72 / 10.11 = 0.269. Note the model's own opinion between legal options is untouched; only illegal ones are removed.

Cost of the mask. The mask is a boolean per vocabulary entry. For a 128,000-token vocabulary packed as bits, that is 128,000 / 8 = 16,000 bytes (about 15.6 KiB) per step per sequence. Engines compute it on the CPU or GPU and apply it with one fused operation, so the overhead is small compared with the model forward pass, provided the mask is cheap to produce (that is the hard part, next sections).

Python (toy masking, runnable with numpy).

import numpy as np

vocab  = ["Sure", "4", "7", "}"]
logits = np.array([3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5])
legal  = np.array([False, True, True, False])  # from the grammar state

def softmax(z):
    e = np.exp(z - z.max())
    return e / e.sum()

masked = np.where(legal, logits, -np.inf)
print(softmax(logits).round(3))   # [0.631 0.232 0.085 0.052]
print(softmax(masked).round(3))   # [0.    0.731 0.269 0.   ]

Kotlin.

import kotlin.math.exp

fun softmax(z: DoubleArray): DoubleArray {
    val m = z.max()
    val e = z.map { exp(it - m) }
    val s = e.sum()
    return e.map { it / s }.toDoubleArray()
}

fun main() {
    val logits = doubleArrayOf(3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5)
    val legal = booleanArrayOf(false, true, true, false)
    val masked = DoubleArray(4) { if (legal[it]) logits[it] else Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY }
    println(softmax(logits).joinToString { "%.3f".format(it) }) // 0.631, 0.232, 0.085, 0.052
    println(softmax(masked).joinToString { "%.3f".format(it) }) // 0.000, 0.731, 0.269, 0.000
}

Java.

public class MaskDemo {
    static double[] softmax(double[] z) {
        double max = Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;
        for (double v : z) max = Math.max(max, v);
        double sum = 0;
        double[] e = new double[z.length];
        for (int i = 0; i < z.length; i++) { e[i] = Math.exp(z[i] - max); sum += e[i]; }
        for (int i = 0; i < z.length; i++) e[i] /= sum;
        return e;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        double[] logits = {3.0, 2.0, 1.0, 0.5};
        boolean[] legal = {false, true, true, false};
        double[] masked = new double[4];
        for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) masked[i] = legal[i] ? logits[i] : Double.NEGATIVE_INFINITY;
        System.out.println(java.util.Arrays.toString(softmax(masked))); // [0.0, 0.731, 0.269, 0.0]
    }
}

The subtraction of the maximum is a standard numerical-stability trick; -inf - max stays -inf and exp(-inf) is 0 in all three languages.

Real life. A multiple-choice test where the invalid options are blacked out before the student picks; the student still prefers their favourite among what is left.

Common interview traps.

  • Setting illegal logits to a large negative number like -100 instead of true minus infinity: usually fine, but it leaves a tiny probability and can leak a bad token when other logits are very low. Engines use -inf.
  • Expecting masking to change the model's weights. It changes only the sampling distribution, per step.
  • If all tokens are masked (grammar dead end), softmax produces NaN. Good engines detect this; it signals a grammar or tokenizer bug.

notes.title: From a schema to an automaton: finite-state machines and regex
notes.html:
Where does the "legal tokens" list come from? From a small state machine built from your schema before generation starts.

Finite-state machine (FSM). A set of states plus rules "in state A, character c moves you to state B". Some states are "accepting" (the text so far is a complete valid answer). A regular expression is exactly a way to describe an FSM. A JSON Schema without recursion can be turned into one regex, then into an FSM. This is the approach of the Outlines paper.

Tiny example. Schema: {"mood": "happy" | "sad"}. Equivalent regex:

\{"mood": ?"(happy|sad)"\}

The FSM walks the characters. After {"mood": "h the only legal continuation is appy"}. After {"mood": " the legal first characters are h or s.

state 0 --'{'--> 1 --'"mood":'--> 2 --'"'--> 3 --'h'--> 4a (then a,p,p,y)
                                             \--'s'--> 4b (then a,d)
                                   ... --'"'--> --'}'--> ACCEPT

Integers and numbers are regexes too: an integer is -?(0|[1-9][0-9]*). A string is "([^"\\]|\\.)*". An array of integers is \[ ?(int(, ?int)*)? ?\].

What FSMs cannot do. Regular languages cannot count unbounded nesting. "Matching brackets to any depth" needs a stack. A schema that refers to itself (a tree node with children that are tree nodes) cannot be a plain regex; you either cap the depth (for example 3 levels, unrolled) or use a grammar with a stack (next section).

Python (the idea, with the standard re module; real engines use their own compiled automata).

import re

pattern = re.compile(r'\{"mood": ?"(happy|sad)"\}')

def is_prefix_possible(text: str) -> bool:
    # toy check: try every completion; real engines walk an FSM instead
    candidates = ['{"mood": "happy"}', '{"mood": "sad"}']
    return any(c.startswith(text) for c in candidates)

print(bool(pattern.fullmatch('{"mood": "sad"}')))  # True
print(is_prefix_possible('{"mood": "s'))             # True
print(is_prefix_possible('{"mood": "x'))             # False

Kotlin.

val pattern = Regex("""\{"mood": ?"(happy|sad)"\}""")
val candidates = listOf("""{"mood": "happy"}""", """{"mood": "sad"}""")

fun prefixPossible(text: String) = candidates.any { it.startsWith(text) }

fun main() {
    println(pattern.matches("""{"mood": "sad"}"""))   // true
    println(prefixPossible("""{"mood": "s"""))          // true
    println(prefixPossible("""{"mood": "x"""))          // false
}

Java.

import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public class PrefixDemo {
    static final Pattern P = Pattern.compile("\\{\"mood\": ?\"(happy|sad)\"\\}");
    static final List<String> CANDIDATES = List.of("{\"mood\": \"happy\"}", "{\"mood\": \"sad\"}");

    static boolean prefixPossible(String t) {
        return CANDIDATES.stream().anyMatch(c -> c.startsWith(t));
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(P.matcher("{\"mood\": \"sad\"}").matches()); // true
        System.out.println(prefixPossible("{\"mood\": \"x"));            // false
    }
}

These snippets only demonstrate the "is this prefix still completable" question. Production engines never enumerate completions; they keep a current automaton state and look up the legal set for it.

Real life. A turnstile maze: at each junction only certain doors open, and you can only reach the exit by following valid doors.

Common interview traps.

  • "A regex can validate any JSON." No: arbitrary-depth nesting is not regular. Real JSON needs a pushdown grammar or a depth cap.
  • Forgetting whitespace. A regex that forbids spaces forces ugly compact output; one that allows unbounded whitespace invites degenerate loops (see failure patterns).
  • Assuming optional fields cost nothing: optional fields multiply the number of states and the compile time.

notes.title: Context-free grammars, GBNF and nested structures
notes.html:
What it is. A context-free grammar (CFG) is a set of rewrite rules such as value := object | array | string | number, where rules may call themselves. That recursion gives the stack that nesting needs. Generation then needs a pushdown automaton: an FSM plus a stack that remembers which brackets are open.

Why you want it. (a) Real JSON with arbitrary nesting. (b) Non-JSON targets: SQL, a small DSL, a function-call syntax, YAML, Python expressions, arithmetic, an Android layout language. If you can write the grammar, the model can only emit programs that parse.

GBNF (llama.cpp's grammar format). Rules look like name ::= alternatives. A tiny grammar that forces a yes/no/maybe answer followed by a number from 1 to 5:

root   ::= answer " " score
answer ::= "yes" | "no" | "maybe"
score  ::= [1-5]

llama.cpp also ships a JSON grammar and a converter from JSON Schema to GBNF (json_schema_to_grammar; verify the exact script and flag names in the llama.cpp repo, as they evolve).

How the engine uses it at each step.

  1. Keep the parser state (which rule, how deep in the stack).
  2. For each vocabulary token, ask "could this token's characters be consumed from this state without a dead end?".
  3. Mark those tokens legal; mask the rest.
  4. Sample a token, advance the parser by the token's characters.
  5. Stop when the grammar reaches an accepting state and the model emits end-of-sequence (EOS is itself a token that is legal only in accepting states).

Step 2 naively costs O(vocabulary) parser trials per step (128,000 trial runs), which is too slow; the next section is about making it fast.

Python (llama-cpp-python grammar, verify class names in its docs).

from llama_cpp import Llama, LlamaGrammar

grammar = LlamaGrammar.from_string('''
root   ::= answer " " score
answer ::= "yes" | "no" | "maybe"
score  ::= [1-5]
''')
llm = Llama(model_path="model.gguf")
out = llm("Is the sky blue? Answer and score 1-5: ", grammar=grammar, max_tokens=8)
print(out["choices"][0]["text"])   # e.g. "yes 5"

Kotlin. No official llama.cpp binding with grammars on the JVM that I can cite with confidence; the practical route is calling a running llama-server over HTTP and passing the grammar field in the JSON body (field name from the llama.cpp server docs; verify):

import java.net.URI
import java.net.http.*

fun main() {
    val gbnf = "root ::= (\\\"yes\\\" | \\\"no\\\" | \\\"maybe\\\") \\\" \\\" [1-5]"
    val body = """{"prompt":"Is the sky blue? ","n_predict":8,"grammar":"$gbnf"}"""
    val req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI("http://localhost:8080/completion"))
        .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build()
    println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body())
}

Java.

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class GrammarCall {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String gbnf = "root ::= (\\\"yes\\\" | \\\"no\\\" | \\\"maybe\\\") \\\" \\\" [1-5]";
        String body = "{\"prompt\":\"Is the sky blue? \",\"n_predict\":8,\"grammar\":\"" + gbnf + "\"}";
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("http://localhost:8080/completion"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
    }
}

Real life. A grammar is the rulebook of a board game; the model can choose any move, but only from the legal-move list the rulebook computes for the current board.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a grammar guarantees meaning. yes 5 is valid even if the true answer is no.
  • Left-recursive or highly ambiguous grammars make parsing slow or loop; write grammars right-recursive and tight.
  • Forgetting that EOS must be reachable. A grammar with no accepting state makes the model run until max_tokens.

notes.title: The tokenizer mismatch problem and how engines make it fast
notes.html:
This is the part that separates a toy demo from a real engine, and it is a favourite senior question.

The mismatch. Grammars talk about characters. The model talks about tokens, and one token spans several characters. The tokenizer might have a token for ": and another for ", : separately. The same text can be tokenised several ways. A token is legal if all its characters walk the automaton without dead-ending, possibly crossing several grammar rules in one token (for example the single token "} closes a string and an object).

Naive approach cost. 128,000 tokens times several characters per step is hundreds of thousands of automaton moves, per generated token. Too slow for serving.

Index precomputation (Outlines idea). Before generation, for every automaton state, precompute which vocabulary tokens are legal and which state each leads to. At run time the lookup is one dictionary access: legal = index[state]. Cost moves to compile time, memory grows with (states times legal tokens).

Adaptive mask caching (XGrammar idea). For pushdown grammars the stack makes full precomputation impossible. XGrammar splits tokens into those whose validity depends only on the current state (cached ahead of time as a bitmask) and a small "context-dependent" set that is checked at run time against the actual stack. The paper reports large speedups over earlier engines; treat the exact multipliers as "verify in the paper".

Alignment and token healing. If the prompt ends mid-token (for example in http:) forcing the grammar on an unaligned boundary can steer the model to unnatural tokenisations and worse text. Guidance's token healing backs up one token and lets the model regenerate it under the constraint.

Fast-forward (jump-forward) decoding. If the grammar leaves exactly one legal continuation (for example the key name "customer_id": ), there is no choice to sample. Some engines insert those tokens directly without running the model for each, saving forward passes. SGLang calls this jump-forward decoding. This is an actual speed win: structured output can be faster than free text.

Python (precomputed index, toy tokenizer).

# tiny vocab; the grammar is the single string  {"ok":true}
vocab = ['{"', 'ok', '":', 'true', '}', '{', '"', ':', 'x']
target = '{"ok":true}'

# index[pos] = tokens legal when `pos` characters of target are already written
index = {}
for pos in range(len(target)):
    index[pos] = [t for t in vocab if target.startswith(t, pos)]

print(index[0])  # ['{"', '{']
print(index[2])  # ['ok']

Kotlin.

val vocab = listOf("{\"", "ok", "\":", "true", "}", "{", "\"", ":", "x")
val target = "{\"ok\":true}"

fun main() {
    val index = (0 until target.length).associateWith { pos -> vocab.filter { target.startsWith(it, pos) } }
    println(index[0]) // [{", {]
    println(index[2]) // [ok]
}

Java.

import java.util.*;
import java.util.stream.*;

public class IndexDemo {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        List<String> vocab = List.of("{\"", "ok", "\":", "true", "}", "{", "\"", ":", "x");
        String target = "{\"ok\":true}";
        Map<Integer, List<String>> index = new HashMap<>();
        for (int pos = 0; pos < target.length(); pos++) {
            int p = pos;
            index.put(p, vocab.stream().filter(t -> target.startsWith(t, p)).collect(Collectors.toList()));
        }
        System.out.println(index.get(0)); // [{", {]
        System.out.println(index.get(2)); // [ok]
    }
}

Note the toy only handles one fixed string; the point is that legality is decided per vocabulary token against the characters remaining, and the result can be cached per state. Also note that at position 0 both {" and { are legal even though they produce different token sequences for the same text.

Real life. A railway timetable printed in advance: instead of computing the route live for every passenger, you look up the departures from this station.

Common interview traps.

  • "Constrained decoding works on characters." It works on tokens; the character grammar is lifted onto the token vocabulary.
  • Mismatching the tokenizer: compiling the grammar against a different tokenizer than the model's gives wrong masks. The grammar compiler must be built from the exact model vocabulary.
  • Expecting the constraint to be free. Compile time and mask memory are real costs, but per-step overhead of a good engine is small.

notes.title: Engines and providers: who offers what
notes.html:
You rarely write this yourself. You pick a layer.

Layer Examples How you use it
Hosted API structured outputs OpenAI (response_format with json_schema, strict: true), Gemini (responseSchema / responseMimeType), Anthropic (verify current structured-output feature and parameters in docs) Pass a JSON Schema; the provider runs the constraint
Strict tool calling OpenAI strict function schemas, Anthropic tools Constrains tool arguments; verify per provider
Self-hosted serving vLLM guided decoding (backends such as Outlines, XGrammar, lm-format-enforcer; verify which are default in your version), SGLang, TGI grammars, llama.cpp, Ollama format Parameter in the request: JSON schema, regex, choice list, or grammar
Libraries Outlines, Guidance, LMQL, Instructor (retry-based, not constrained), Pydantic-based wrappers Python-side orchestration

JSON mode vs schema mode. JSON mode guarantees syntactically valid JSON only. Schema mode guarantees your schema. Check which one a flag means; many bugs come from assuming the stronger one.

Which JSON Schema features work? Providers support a subset. Commonly restricted: recursion depth, oneOf/anyOf combinations, pattern regexes, numeric bounds like minimum/maximum, string lengths, additionalProperties rules (strict modes often require additionalProperties: false and all fields listed as required). This changes frequently; always verify in the provider docs.

Python (OpenAI-compatible endpoint, works for OpenAI and for vLLM; schema mode).

import os
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(api_key=os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"])  # base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1" for vLLM
schema = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
        "reasoning": {"type": "string"},
        "priority": {"type": "string", "enum": ["HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW"]},
    },
    "required": ["reasoning", "priority"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4.1-mini",  # verify model id
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Ticket: app crashes at login for all users"}],
    response_format={"type": "json_schema",
                     "json_schema": {"name": "ticket", "strict": True, "schema": schema}},
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)  # {"reasoning":"...","priority":"HIGH"}
print(resp.choices[0].finish_reason)    # check "stop", not "length"

Kotlin (plain REST with OkHttp; same endpoint, same body).

import okhttp3.*
import okhttp3.MediaType.Companion.toMediaType
import okhttp3.RequestBody.Companion.toRequestBody

fun main() {
    val body = """
      {"model":"gpt-4.1-mini",
       "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Ticket: app crashes at login"}],
       "response_format":{"type":"json_schema","json_schema":{"name":"ticket","strict":true,
         "schema":{"type":"object","properties":{
            "reasoning":{"type":"string"},
            "priority":{"type":"string","enum":["HIGH","MEDIUM","LOW"]}},
          "required":["reasoning","priority"],"additionalProperties":false}}}}
    """.trimIndent()
    val req = Request.Builder().url("https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions")
        .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
        .post(body.toRequestBody("application/json".toMediaType())).build()
    OkHttpClient().newCall(req).execute().use { println(it.body?.string()) }
}

On Android, do not ship the key: call your own backend, which makes this request and returns the typed result.

Java (java.net.http).

import java.net.URI;
import java.net.http.*;

public class StructuredCall {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String body = """
          {"model":"gpt-4.1-mini",
           "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Ticket: app crashes at login"}],
           "response_format":{"type":"json_schema","json_schema":{"name":"ticket","strict":true,
             "schema":{"type":"object","properties":{
                "reasoning":{"type":"string"},
                "priority":{"type":"string","enum":["HIGH","MEDIUM","LOW"]}},
              "required":["reasoning","priority"],"additionalProperties":false}}}}
          """;
        HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions"))
            .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + System.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))
            .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString(body)).build();
        System.out.println(HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).body());
    }
}

For Anthropic the same idea may be available through its own parameter (verify in the Anthropic API docs and the anthropic / anthropic-java SDK reference) or, as a long-standing alternative, a single forced tool whose input_schema is your schema. For vLLM, the request carries the schema via an extra body field (guided_json in older versions, a structured_outputs option in newer ones; verify for your version).

Real life. Choosing between ordering from a set menu (hosted API), cooking in your own kitchen with a recipe card (self-hosted engine), or writing your own recipe system (a library).

Common interview traps.

  • Using JSON mode and calling it "guaranteed schema".
  • Sending a schema feature the provider does not support and getting either a 400 error or a silent loosening; read the supported subset.
  • Using Instructor-style libraries and assuming they use masking; many validate and retry instead (different guarantee, different cost).

notes.title: Quality trade-offs: does forcing the format make answers worse?
notes.html:
Constraints guarantee shape. They can hurt content in four ways.

1. Distribution distortion. Masking renormalises probabilities token by token (greedy-per-step), which is not the same as sampling from "the model's distribution restricted to valid whole outputs". Consider a model that wants to write "colour" but the enum only allows "color". Step by step, once "c is forced, the model's mass on the continuations may be tiny and weird, and a bad path can get picked even though a different whole-answer would have been more probable. Research on this ("sampling bias" in grammar-aligned decoding; verify the paper name and authors before citing) shows such distortions exist. In practice it matters mostly for small models and for tightly restricted grammars.

2. Reasoning cut off. If the schema is {"answer": "B"} the model has no room to think. Accuracy on reasoning tasks can drop versus free chain-of-thought. Several write-ups and papers (for example "Let Me Speak Freely?", 2024; verify) report format restrictions lowering reasoning performance, with strictness mattering. The fix is cheap: put a reasoning string field before the answer field so tokens spent on thinking come first.

Bad:   {"answer": "...", "explanation": "..."}     <- answer chosen before any thinking
Good:  {"reasoning": "...", "answer": "..."}       <- thinking tokens come first

3. Key order and field names are prompt. The model reads the field names and descriptions as instructions. A field called x1 with no description gets worse values than invoice_total_usd with "Total including tax, in US dollars, as a number".

4. Forced hallucination. If a field is required and the text does not contain the value, the model must produce something well-formed, so it invents. Allow null, add an "unknown" enum member, or make fields optional with the rule "null if not stated".

Cost and latency numbers. There is no universal number. Extra input tokens come from the schema (a 30-field schema may be a few hundred tokens: count it, do not guess), grammar compile happens once per new schema, then is cached (providers document first-request latency; verify). Output tokens can go up (keys and punctuation are tokens) or down (no apologies, no retries). Always measure p50 and p95 on your own schema.

Python (reasoning-first schema as a Pydantic model, then validate).

from typing import Literal, Optional
from pydantic import BaseModel

class Decision(BaseModel):
    reasoning: str                      # think first
    category: Literal["BILLING", "TECH", "OTHER"]
    order_id: Optional[str] = None      # null instead of inventing

print(Decision.model_json_schema()["required"])  # ['reasoning', 'category']

Kotlin (kotlinx.serialization data class; field order is declaration order).

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

enum class Category { BILLING, TECH, OTHER }

@Serializable
data class Decision(val reasoning: String, val category: Category, val orderId: String? = null)

fun main() {
    val d = Json.decodeFromString<Decision>("""{"reasoning":"card charged twice","category":"BILLING"}""")
    println(d) // Decision(reasoning=card charged twice, category=BILLING, orderId=null)
}

Java (record + Jackson).

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;

public class DecisionDemo {
    enum Category { BILLING, TECH, OTHER }
    record Decision(String reasoning, Category category, String orderId) {}

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        var d = new ObjectMapper().readValue(
            "{\"reasoning\":\"card charged twice\",\"category\":\"BILLING\"}", Decision.class);
        System.out.println(d); // Decision[reasoning=card charged twice, category=BILLING, orderId=null]
    }
}

Real life. A strict exam form that has only an answer box: students who would have shown their working now guess. Add a "working" box above the answer.

Common interview traps.

  • "Constrained decoding guarantees correct answers." It guarantees shape only; correctness still needs validation, evaluation and grounding.
  • Putting the final answer key first in the schema and wondering why accuracy dropped.
  • Assuming structured output is always slower. Fast-forwarded boilerplate tokens and avoided retries often make it faster.

notes.title: Production failure patterns
notes.html:
Real incidents and how to spot them.

1. Truncation (finish_reason: length). The model hits max_tokens halfway through a valid prefix. Constrained decoding only guarantees every emitted prefix is legal, not that the output finished. The result is invalid JSON with no closing bracket. Always check the finish/stop reason, set max_tokens generously, and treat length as an error, not a success.

2. Whitespace or digit runaway. A grammar that allows unlimited spaces or newlines between tokens lets a model fall into a loop that emits whitespace forever (it is legal, and some models like it). Same with unbounded string or number length. Fixes: bound whitespace in the grammar (many engines default to a small cap or "no extra whitespace" mode), set max_tokens, set stop conditions.

3. Refusal and safety outputs. A safety refusal may arrive in a separate field or not match your schema. Handle a refusal field or a non-schema stop reason (provider specific; verify). Do not blindly parse(content).

4. Schema rejected or silently weakened. Unsupported keyword gives a 400 on one provider and is ignored on another. After a model or provider upgrade the supported subset can change. Keep a contract test that sends your real schema through and checks that an invalid candidate is truly impossible.

5. Compile latency spikes. A new or dynamic schema (generated per user) forces a fresh grammar compile each time and misses the cache. Symptoms: p95 latency jumps on first request after deploy; huge numbers of unique schemas. Fix: use a small fixed set of schemas, warm the cache at startup, and avoid per-request schema generation.

6. Dead-end grammar. A bug where the grammar can reach a state with no legal token. Engines either raise an error or emit garbage; test grammars with a generator that tries to enumerate samples.

7. Tokenizer drift. You upgrade the model, the vocabulary changes, but a cached compiled grammar from the old tokenizer is reused. Key the cache by (schema hash, tokenizer id).

8. Wrong but valid values. Dates like 2026-13-45 pass a string type but are not dates. Use format-specific patterns where supported and always validate semantically on your side (business rules, ranges, references to real ids).

9. Streaming parse. If you stream tokens to a UI, a partial JSON is not parseable. Use an incremental JSON parser or stream per field. Constrained output makes incremental parsing safer, since every prefix is valid.

Python (defensive wrapper: finish reason, parse, semantic check, one retry).

import json
from datetime import date

def call_and_check(call) -> dict:
    for attempt in range(2):
        resp = call()  # returns an object like the chat completion above
        choice = resp.choices[0]
        if choice.finish_reason != "stop":          # "length" -> truncated
            continue
        try:
            data = json.loads(choice.message.content)
            date.fromisoformat(data["due_date"])    # semantic check beyond the schema
            return data
        except (ValueError, KeyError):
            continue
    raise RuntimeError("structured output failed validation after retry")

Kotlin.

import kotlinx.serialization.json.*
import java.time.LocalDate

fun checked(finishReason: String, content: String): JsonObject? {
    if (finishReason != "stop") return null            // "length" means truncated
    return try {
        val obj = Json.parseToJsonElement(content).jsonObject
        LocalDate.parse(obj["due_date"]!!.jsonPrimitive.content) // semantic check
        obj
    } catch (e: Exception) { null }
}

Java.

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.*;
import java.time.LocalDate;

public class Checked {
    static JsonNode checked(String finishReason, String content) {
        if (!"stop".equals(finishReason)) return null;      // truncated
        try {
            JsonNode n = new ObjectMapper().readTree(content);
            LocalDate.parse(n.get("due_date").asText());     // semantic check
            return n;
        } catch (Exception e) { return null; }
    }
}

Real life. A vending machine that guarantees the item falls into the tray in a valid shape, but cannot guarantee the tray is not empty because someone unplugged it halfway (truncation).

Common interview traps.

  • Logging only the parsed object: log the raw text, finish reason and schema hash too, or you cannot debug.
  • Treating constrained decoding as a replacement for validation. Keep both (defence in depth).
  • Caching grammars without tokenizer identity in the key.

notes.title: Beyond JSON: regex, choices, and tool arguments
notes.html:
The same mask can enforce many targets.

  • Choice / classification. Allowed outputs are a fixed list: ["positive", "negative", "neutral"]. Often the first token already decides the class, so you can also read the logits directly and get a calibrated-ish score instead of sampling; this is a cheap, fast classifier pattern (verify calibration on your data).
  • Regex. Phone numbers, order ids like ORD-[0-9]{6}, ISO dates \d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}. Good for single fields. Regex still cannot check that the month is 1 to 12 unless you write that too.
  • Code and query languages. A grammar for a SQL subset (only SELECT from allowed tables) greatly reduces broken or dangerous queries. It is not a security boundary by itself: still use a read-only database user and parameterise.
  • Tool calling arguments. A strict function schema means argument names and types always match your function signature. The model still can choose the wrong tool or wrong values; that is a reasoning problem, not a syntax problem.
  • Agents and planning formats. Constrain each step to {"thought": ..., "action": enum, "input": ...} to keep the loop parseable.
  • On-device models. MediaPipe LLM Inference and similar runtimes on Android: check whether they expose grammar or JSON constraints (verify; many on-device stacks lack them), otherwise prompt for the format and validate with retry.

Python (choice constraint with vLLM-style OpenAI client; parameter name varies by version, verify).

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="unused")
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="my-model",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Review: battery dies in an hour"}],
    extra_body={"guided_choice": ["positive", "negative", "neutral"]},  # newer vLLM: structured_outputs
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)  # negative

Kotlin (client-side fallback when the engine has no constraints: validate against an allowed set).

val allowed = setOf("positive", "negative", "neutral")

fun normalise(raw: String): String? = raw.trim().lowercase().takeIf { it in allowed }

fun main() {
    println(normalise(" Negative\n")) // negative
    println(normalise("kind of bad")) // null -> retry or fall back
}

Java.

import java.util.Set;

public class Choice {
    static final Set<String> ALLOWED = Set.of("positive", "negative", "neutral");

    static String normalise(String raw) {
        String s = raw.trim().toLowerCase();
        return ALLOWED.contains(s) ? s : null;
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println(normalise(" Negative\n")); // negative
        System.out.println(normalise("kind of bad")); // null
    }
}

Real life. A ballot paper: you may only tick one of the printed candidates, no write-ins.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing a SQL grammar makes generated SQL safe. It controls syntax and vocabulary, not semantics or permissions.
  • Using a choice constraint on a vague label set; the model will pick something even if none fits, so include other or unknown.
  • Assuming on-device runtimes support grammars. Check before designing around it.

notes.title: Choosing an approach: a decision guide
notes.html:
Use this as the answer to "how would you get reliable structured data from an LLM?".

Need machine-readable output?
  no  -> free text.
  yes -> Is the endpoint under your control (self-hosted)?
           yes -> use the engine's guided decoding (schema / regex / grammar).
           no  -> does the provider offer strict schema mode?
                    yes -> use it; keep schema inside the supported subset.
                    no  -> strict tool call, or prompt + examples + validate + retry (max 2).
  Always: reasoning field first, nullable unknowns, finish-reason check, semantic validation,
          contract test on upgrades, log raw output.

Cost reasoning example (show your math). Suppose the retry-based approach fails syntactically 3 percent of the time and each call costs 1 unit. Expected calls per success are 1 / (1 - 0.03) = 1.031, so about 3.1 percent extra spend, plus tail latency on the retried ones. Constrained decoding removes that 3.1 percent but may add a schema of, say, 300 input tokens (count it for your schema) on every call. If the prompt is already 2,000 tokens, 300 more is 15 percent more input. So the cheaper choice depends on your numbers: measure both; with prompt caching the schema cost can drop (verify provider caching rules).

Python (measure, don't guess: count schema tokens, tokenizer-specific).

import json
import tiktoken  # OpenAI-style tokenizer; use the right tokenizer for your model

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
schema = {"type": "object", "properties": {"priority": {"enum": ["HIGH", "LOW"]}}}
print(len(enc.encode(json.dumps(schema))))  # token count of the schema text

Kotlin. There is no equally standard tokenizer library on the JVM that matches provider tokenizers; use the provider's token-counting endpoint (verify: Anthropic and Gemini offer token counting APIs) or a JVM port such as jtokkit for OpenAI encodings (verify its API).

// pseudo-usage, verify jtokkit API before relying on it
// val enc = Encodings.newDefaultEncodingRegistry().getEncoding(EncodingType.CL100K_BASE)
// println(enc.countTokens(schemaJson))

Java.

// pseudo-usage with jtokkit, verify the API in its README
// EncodingRegistry registry = Encodings.newDefaultEncodingRegistry();
// Encoding enc = registry.getEncoding(EncodingType.CL100K_BASE);
// System.out.println(enc.countTokens(schemaJson));

Real life. Choosing between a pre-printed form (constrained decoding, small fixed cost per page) and hand-checking free-form letters (retries, human cost per error).

Common interview traps.

  • Answering only "use JSON mode". A senior answer lists the guarantee ladder, validation, truncation checks and monitoring.
  • Quoting precise speedups or prices from memory; say "measure and verify".
  • Ignoring that the cheapest fix is sometimes a simpler schema, not a smarter engine.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Models emit tokens one at a time, so valid format is only likely, never guaranteed. Constrained decoding makes it guaranteed by editing the sampling step.
  • Mechanism: at each step compute the legal next tokens from a grammar state, set other logits to negative infinity, renormalise, sample. In the worked example, P(Sure) 0.631 became 0 and the digits renormalised to 0.731 and 0.269.
  • Regex and finite-state machines handle flat schemas; context-free grammars with a stack handle arbitrary nesting and non-JSON targets such as SQL (GBNF in llama.cpp).
  • The hard engineering is the character-versus-token mismatch: engines precompute per-state token masks (Outlines index, XGrammar adaptive cache) and may jump-forward over forced text.
  • Offerings: hosted strict schema modes, strict tool calling, self-hosted vLLM/SGLang/llama.cpp, and libraries. JSON mode is weaker than schema mode; supported schema subsets differ and change (verify).
  • Trade-offs: guaranteed shape, not truth; possible distribution distortion; reasoning loss if the answer comes first, so put a reasoning field first; use nullable fields and an unknown option to avoid forced hallucination.
  • Production failures: truncation (check finish reason), whitespace loops, refusals, unsupported schema features, compile latency, tokenizer-keyed caches, valid-but-wrong values. Keep semantic validation, a contract test, and raw-output logging.
  • Unverified in this note and marked "verify": exact Anthropic structured-output parameter names, vLLM request field names by version, llama.cpp server and binding details, XGrammar speedup figures, and the research paper titles cited.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming constrained decoding "solves hallucination". It solves syntax.
  • Forgetting truncation, refusals and semantic validation.
  • Not being able to explain the logit mask and the token-versus-character problem in two sentences.
